name: Messages to Mars
short_status: The deliberate messages are still there, from a Soviet pennant that arrived as wreckage on 27 November 1971 to flags, memorial plaques, four sundials, a 1909 penny and a parachute encoding DARE MIGHTY THINGS. One plaque meant for Mars is still in a museum in Washington.
tagline: USSR, NASA, ESA and CNSA · Multinational · Artefact · 2021 · Multipolar Mars Success
stats: the first deliberate message delivered, a pennant with the Soviet coat of arms, arriving as wreckage
sundials landed on Mars, each carrying a motto: Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity and Perseverance
imprints of the character zhong stamped into Utopia Planitia by Zhurong's rear wheels

facts.label: The first object with nothing to do
facts.value: NASA's catalogue entry for the Mars 2 descent module lists its cameras, mass spectrometer, weather and soil instruments, and then adds that it also contained a pennant with the Soviet coat of arms. That capsule hit Mars on 27 November 1971 after its parachute sequence never ran, which makes the pennant the first thing humans deliberately placed on the planet and also a piece of debris.

facts.label: The second pennant
facts.value: Russian Wikipedia's Mars 3 article states plainly that a pennant bearing the State Emblem of the USSR was fixed to the descent module, in the same sentence group that records the capsule's pre-flight sterilisation. Mars 3 landed intact on 2 December 1971, so this pennant is the first message delivered to Mars by a working landing. No source we consulted gives its size, shape or material.

facts.label: Pennants that never arrived
facts.value: The practice predates the landing. A letter from Leonid Smirnov, chairman of the Military Industrial Commission, to the Central Committee on 28 November 1964, two days before the launch of Zond 2, states that the flight was to test 3MV hardware, do interplanetary science and, if everything worked, impact Mars and deliver commemorative pennants. Nothing in the 1962 or 1964 series reached the planet.

facts.label: Not on the 1973 landers
facts.value: Russian Wikipedia's article on Mars 6, which reached the atmosphere and lost contact during descent on 12 March 1974, describes the descent module's instruments in detail and mentions no pennant or commemorative object at all. We found no source recording pennants on the Mars 4 to Mars 7 series.

facts.label: Viking, 1976
facts.value: The Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum, writing for the fiftieth anniversary in July 2026, records that the Viking 1 lander that touched down on 20 July 1976 carried the United States flag and the nation's Bicentennial logo. Viking was the United States' Bicentennial mission to Mars, launched in the year the country turned two hundred. The museum's account does not say where on the lander the two markings were fixed.

facts.label: The Viking microdot
facts.value: Jon Lomberg, writing for The Planetary Society, states that each Viking lander carried a tiny dot of microfilm recording the names of several thousand people who had worked on the mission. English Wikipedia repeats his sentence. We have not found a NASA document that describes this microdot, so treat it as an assertion by a well-placed participant rather than a confirmed inventory item.

facts.label: The plaque still on Earth
facts.value: In January 1981 NASA renamed the Viking 1 landing site the Thomas A. Mutch Memorial Station, for the planetary geologist who had led the lander imaging team and who disappeared climbing in the Himalaya. A stainless steel plaque was made, inscribed "Dedicated to the memory of Tim Mutch, whose imagination, verve, and resolve contributed greatly to the exploration of the Solar System." On 18 May 1984 NASA Administrator James M. Beggs handed it to the National Air and Space Museum, which was to retain, secure and protect it until astronauts could affix it to the lander on Mars. The museum still has it.

facts.label: A memorial that is only a name
facts.value: On 5 July 1997, at Planetfest in Pasadena, NASA Administrator Daniel S. Goldin named the Mars Pathfinder lander the Carl Sagan Memorial Station, six months after Sagan's death. The release describes a renaming and no object: nothing was carried to Mars for it. Several Martian memorials work this way, including Columbia Memorial Station and Challenger Memorial Station.

facts.label: Columbia and Challenger
facts.value: An aluminium plaque about six inches across, designed by JPL rover engineers Chris Voorhees and Peter Illsley, was fitted to the back of Spirit's high-gain antenna on 28 March 2003 at the Kennedy Space Center, honouring the STS-107 crew lost on 1 February 2003. NASA Administrator Sean O'Keefe named Spirit's landing site Columbia Memorial Station on 6 January 2004, and named Opportunity's landing site Challenger Memorial Station on 28 January 2004. The plaque rode with the rover, so it lies wherever Spirit stopped. The station that bears the name is a different place.

facts.label: Signatures
facts.value: Curiosity carries an anodised aluminium plaque 100 mm tall by 82 mm wide, bolted to the front left of the rover deck, bearing the signatures of United States officials including President Obama and Vice President Biden. The rover photographed it with MAHLI on sol 44, 19 September 2012. NASA's caption notes that similar signature plaques, including those of the sitting president and vice-president of the day, are on the lander platforms of Spirit and Opportunity, and points to PIA05034 as an image of Spirit's.

facts.label: The sundials
facts.value: The MarsDial began as a conversation between Jim Bell and Bill Nye in 1998 about the shadow-casting post on a camera calibration target. The Spirit and Opportunity version is 8 cm square, weighs 65 g, has a 2 cm sphere as its nodus, carries the motto "Two Worlds, One Sun" and the year 2004, and has the name of Mars written around it. Sullivan and Bell say 17 languages; English Wikipedia says 22. We found no NASA caption we could cite for either figure. Four sides carry a short message and drawings inspired by schoolchildren's suggestions.

facts.label: What the later sundials say
facts.value: Curiosity's dial, assembled at the University of Washington and about three inches square, reads "To Mars To Explore". The University of Washington account traces the year plates rather than giving Curiosity's: the seven dials made in 1999 read "Mars 2002" for a lander that was then cancelled, and were slip-covered to 2004 for the Mars Exploration Rovers. Its four sides carry a compressed history of how humans have seen Mars, ending: "Through it all, we have wondered: Has there been life on Mars? To those taking the next steps to find out, we wish a safe journey and the joy of discovery." Perseverance's Mastcam-Z target reads "Two Worlds, One Beginning", and around its outer edge: "Are we alone? We came here to look for signs of life, and to collect samples of Mars for study on Earth. To those who follow, we wish a safe journey and the joy of discovery." The phrase Joy of Discovery is repeated around it in several languages.

facts.label: Things smuggled onto calibration targets
facts.value: Curiosity's MAHLI calibration target carries a 1909 VDB Lincoln penny, both as a scale reference of the kind geologists use and as a nod to the coin's centenary. Perseverance's SHERLOC target carries a slice of the Martian meteorite Sayh al Uhaymir 008, five swatches of spacesuit material being watched for degradation, and a coin cut from helmet visor material inscribed with the address of Sherlock Holmes, placed there as a geocache. NASA's captions render the meteorite name as both SaU 008 and SaH 008.

facts.label: Writing on the ground
facts.value: Curiosity's wheel treads carry a hole pattern that spells JPL in Morse code, adopted after NASA declined to let the laboratory's initials be written on the wheels as text; the pattern is used to measure slip. Zhurong's two rear wheels carry the character zhong, so the rover stamped it into southern Utopia Planitia as it drove. Xinhua reported on 16 January 2023 that it had left nearly 4,000 of them over more than 1,900 metres. Deputy chief designer Jia Yang has described the spacing of the characters as a slip diagnostic as well as a commemoration.

facts.label: The parachute
facts.value: Perseverance's supersonic parachute was woven in a pattern that encodes, in binary, the words DARE MIGHTY THINGS across its inner rings and the coordinates of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory around its outer band. It was designed by Mars 2020 systems engineer Ian Clark, and members of the public decoded it from descent imagery within days of the landing on 18 February 2021. The parachute and backshell were cut away during descent and are still lying on the surface of Jezero crater, separately from the rover.

facts.label: A piece of the first aeroplane
facts.value: A 1.3 cm square of unbleached Pride of the West muslin, cut from the covering of the Wright brothers' Flyer of 1903 and supplied by Carillon Historical Park in Dayton, Ohio, was sealed in polyamide film and attached to a cable under the solar panel of the Ingenuity helicopter. It is now at Valinor Hills, where Ingenuity made its final landing.

timeline: Two days before Zond 2 launches, a letter from the chairman of the Military Industrial Commission sets out the mission's real objectives, which include impacting Mars and delivering commemorative pennants. The spacecraft dies on the way.

The Mars 2 descent module strikes Mars with its parachute sequence unrun. The pennant bearing the Soviet coat of arms bolted to it becomes the first object humans deliberately placed on the surface of another planet, and has never been located.
Mars 3 lands intact carrying the same emblem, delivering the first Martian message by a working landing. It transmits for seconds and stops.

Viking 1 lands in Chryse Planitia carrying a United States flag and the Bicentennial logo of a country celebrating its two hundredth year, along with, by Jon Lomberg's account, a microfilm dot of the names of people who built it.
NASA renames the Viking 1 landing site the Thomas A. Mutch Memorial Station and has a stainless steel plaque made for it. The plaque cannot be delivered, because nothing is going there.

NASA Administrator James M. Beggs gives the Mutch plaque to the National Air and Space Museum, with instructions to hold it until astronauts can fix it to the lander, and transfers ownership of Viking 1 on Mars to the museum in the same letter.
NASA Administrator Daniel S. Goldin names the Pathfinder lander the Carl Sagan Memorial Station. Nothing physical is involved: the memorial is the name.

Beagle 2 lands in Isidis Planitia carrying a Damien Hirst spot painting as its instrument calibration chart and a call sign composed by members of Blur. Neither is ever seen or heard from the surface.

Spirit and Opportunity land carrying MarsDials inscribed "Two Worlds, One Sun", signature chips, signature plaques on their lander platforms, Columbia memorial plaques on their high-gain antennas and rock abrasion tool shields machined from World Trade Center aluminium. NASA names the two landing sites Columbia Memorial Station on 6 January and Challenger Memorial Station on 28 January.

Curiosity lands in Gale crater with a 1909 penny on its arm camera target, a sundial reading "To Mars To Explore", a signed plaque on its deck, Morse code in its wheels and a micro-reproduction of Leonardo da Vinci's Codex on the Flight of Birds fastened to a names chip.
Perseverance lands in Jezero crater. Within days the public has decoded DARE MIGHTY THINGS from the parachute in the descent imagery, and NASA publishes an annotated key.

Zhurong lands in southern Utopia Planitia and drives 1,921 m before hibernating. Xinhua reports in January 2023 that its rear wheels have stamped nearly 4,000 copies of the character zhong into the ground on the way.

images.caption: A six kopeck Soviet stamp issued in 1972 and headed Автоматическая станция «Марс-2»: вымпел на планете 27.11.71 г., showing a painted M-71 station firing its engine beside a crescent Mars, with an inset panel at the upper left depicting the pennant itself: a plate carrying the State Emblem of the USSR and the words ЗЕМЛЯ МАРС СССР 1971.
images.credit: Почта СССР (USSR Post); scan by Andrew Butko, via Wikimedia Commons

images.caption: A Spirit navigation camera view of the aluminium memorial plaque bolted to the back of the rover's high-gain antenna, reading IN MEMORIAM, TO THE CREW OF THE SPACE SHUTTLE COLUMBIA, STS-107, FEBRUARY 1, 2003, with the seven crew names, a shuttle silhouette, a United States flag and the NASA insignia, photographed on the surface of Gusev crater.

A framed pair of documents held by the National Air and Space Museum: on the left the 18 May 1984 instrument signed by Walter J. Boyne and NASA Administrator James M. Beggs transferring the Mutch Memorial Station, meaning Viking Lander 1 on Mars, to the museum and charging it to retain, secure and protect the plaque until astronauts can affix it; on the right the Thomas A. Mutch Memorial Station plaque itself, signed by Administrator Robert A. Frosch on 7 January 1981 and carrying the dedication to the memory of Tim Mutch, with a blank line at the foot reading Emplaced.
images.credit: Mark Avino, Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum (NASM2026-01015)

images.caption: Two panoramic camera views of the MarsDial on Spirit's solar deck, taken on Mars near local noon and again later in the afternoon so the shadow of the central post falls differently, with the colour and grey calibration blocks at the corners and the ring of text around the dial.

The primary Mastcam-Z calibration target for the Perseverance rover photographed on Earth before launch, showing the black shadow post at the centre, the grey and colour swatches, and around the rim a fern, an Apatosaurus, a man and a woman raising their hands in greeting, a rocket running from a blue dot to a red dot, a model of the inner solar system, a DNA helix, cyanobacteria and the motto TWO WORLDS, ONE BEGINNING.

A photograph of Perseverance's supersonic parachute taken by an up-look camera on the backshell during the descent to Jezero crater on 18 February 2021, with NASA's annotation overlaid showing how the orange and white gores encode DARE MIGHTY THINGS in binary across the inner rings and the coordinates of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory around the outer band.
